title: Pairwise AI Ranking (PAIR): open parse evaluation
summary: We’re open-sourcing PAIR, the LLM-as-judge framework we use to evaluate document parsers on what matters: whether a parse faithfully preserves the document’s information.
body_markdown:
Evaluating and choosing a document parser is surprisingly difficult. At Reducto, we have spent thousands of hours poring over the long tail of document data, and assessing different ways to scalably and reliably measure the quality of parses. Honing our evaluation methodology has led us to develop industry-leading models like r-1 and r-1 mini that perform well across diverse enterprise use cases. Now, we are publicly releasing our **Pairwise AI Ranking (PAIR)** framework, so everyone can run trustworthy and generalizable parsing evaluations. Our approach focuses on what we found truly matters in practice for preserving document content faithfully. ## Why are parse evaluations hard? Evaluation methodology for document parsing should be unbiased, scalable, and robust across datasets. Most importantly, it must correlate with downstream consequences of parse quality. Existing parse benchmarks rely on deterministic rules or human-labeled ground truth to assess parses. These rules typically codify small subjective judgement calls about how document information should be represented, many of which do not actually impact a human or agent’s understanding of a document’s content. For example, a table can be represented equally well in Markdown or HTML with very little downstream effect, but placing a value under the wrong column header changes its meaning. Strict rules are too brittle to cover edge cases found in real-world documents. One rule checked against three correct outputs. Each output has the same information as the page, but each example rule passes one output and fails the other two. Adjacent tables. Rule: Two tables next to each other on the page must be output as two tables. Two tables: passes. Two tables, same as the page. Section rows: fails. One table. Personal and Business are header rows. Title as header row: fails. One table. The title is the header row. Boxed fields. Rule: Labels and values inside a box must be output as a table. Table: passes. A two-column table. Key-value list: fails. A bulleted list. Each label is next to its value. Plain lines: fails. One line per field. All three fields are there. Equations. Rule: An equation must exactly match a reference LaTeX string. Reference string: passes. Exact match with the reference. Fewer braces: fails. No braces around r and n. Renders the same. Other delimiters: fails. Uses \\\[ \\\] instead of $$. Renders the same. One rule checked against three correct outputs Each output below has the same information as the page. The example rule passes one output and fails the other two. Adjacent tables Boxed fields Equations Policies written (000s) Personal Q1 Q2 Auto 42 45 Home 18 21 Business Q1 Q2 Fleet 7 8 Cyber 3 5 Example rule Two tables next to each other on the page must be output as two tables. ** ** ** 3 of 3 match the page ** ** ** 1 of 3 passes the rule Two tables Passes ```text Policies written (000s) | Personal | Q1 | Q2 | |---|---|---| | Auto | 42 | 45 | | Home | 18 | 21 | | Business | Q1 | Q2 | |---|---|---| | Fleet | 7 | 8 | | Cyber | 3 | 5 | ``` Two tables, same as the page. Section rows Fails ```text Policies written (000s) | | Q1 | Q2 | |---|---|---| | **Personal** | | | | Auto | 42 | 45 | | Home | 18 | 21 | | **Business** | | | | Fleet | 7 | 8 | | Cyber | 3 | 5 | ``` One table. Personal and Business are header rows. Title as header row Fails ```text | Policies written (000s) | | | |---|---|---| | **Personal** | Q1 | Q2 | | Auto | 42 | 45 | | Home | 18 | 21 | | **Business** | Q1 | Q2 | | Fleet | 7 | 8 | | Cyber | 3 | 5 | ``` One table. The title is the header row. The purpose of parsing is to make document information usable by preserving both its content and the relationships that give it meaning. In workflows such as claims processing, financial analysis, and healthcare management, even a single decimal point error can directly affect downstream decisions people and agents make. Parse quality is best assessed by whether or not information is faithfully preserved from a document. That’s why we developed **Pairwise AI Ranking (PAIR)** , an LLM-as-judge methodology focused on assessing content faithfulness and preservation. ## Pairwise AI Ranking (PAIR) PAIR uses an LLM judge to compare two parses of the same page. The judge sees the original page and both parses, then chooses which parse better preserves the document’s information, or declares a tie. We select a shared baseline parser, then run pairwise comparisons between each candidate’s output and the baseline’s output on every benchmark page. We repeat each comparison three times and report win rates with ties counting as half a win. To reduce position bias, we vary which parse appears first across comparisons and hide parser identities from the judge. How PAIR scores a parser. An LLM judge sees the page and two parses of it, one from the parser being tested and one from a baseline parser, and decides which keeps the page’s information better. A win is 1 point, a tie is ½ point and a loss is 0 points. Only markup differs: Both parses have the same values in the same cells. Only the markup is different, so the judge calls it a tie. One value is wrong: The baseline parse has $4,700 where the page says $4,200. The tested parse has every value right, so the tested parser wins. Win rate: 3,000 wins, 1,200 ties and 1,800 losses out of 6,000 judgments give (3,000 + 600 + 0) ÷ 6,000 = 60.0%. How PAIR scores a parser An LLM judge compares the parser’s output with a baseline parser’s output for the same page. The parser gets points when it wins or ties. Only markup differs One value is wrong Page Item Qty Amount Widgets 12 $4,200 Bolts 40 $380 Parser being tested ```text | Item | Qty | Amount | |---------|-----|--------| | Widgets | 12 | $4,200 | | Bolts | 40 | $380 | ``` Baseline parser ```text
ItemQtyAmount
Widgets12$4,200
Bolts40$380
``` LLM judge Which parse keeps the page’s information better? **Win** 1 point **Tie** ½ point **Loss** 0 points Both parses have the same values in the same cells. Only the markup is different, so the judge calls it a tie. The judge does not see parser names, and the order of the two parses is shuffled. Win rate ** ** ** ** 3,000 wins × 1 ** 1,200 ties × ½ ** 1,800 losses × 0 60.0% = (3,000 + 600 + 0) ÷ 6,000 PAIR enables testing of any type of document across any provider without document-specific rules or labeling. In order to build trust in our judge’s behavior, we investigated how closely judge decisions align with human assessments through a third-party human annotation campaign. We submitted the same 300 pairwise comparisons, covering outputs from four parse providers, to both the judge and human reviewers. Each comparison received at least three independent human ratings, followed by review and adjudication to establish a final human verdict. As the results below show, the judge’s decisions align with human verdicts when both choose a winner, with stronger agreement when human reviewers are unanimous. The latter is an especially useful test: when every reviewer identifies the same winner, the judge should have that clear preference too. How often the judge agrees with human raters 300 comparisons of four parsers. At least three people rated each comparison, and their ratings were reviewed to set a final human verdict. Compared with Agreement How it is counted Judge vs. final human verdict, when both pick a winner 84.0% Comparisons where the judge or the humans called a tie are left out. Judge vs. unanimous human verdict, when both pick a winner 91.6% Only comparisons where every human rater picked the same parse. Ties on either side are left out. Judge vs. unanimous human verdict, ties included 72.2% Counts as agreement when both pick the same winner or both call a tie. Judge vs. final human verdict, ties count as agreement 89.7% All comparisons. It only counts as disagreement when the judge and the humans pick different winners. We also tested whether the LLM judge could discern harmless formatting changes from genuinely damaged content. We edited r-1 outputs for 100 pages in controlled ways and asked the judge to compare each edited version with the original, 604 comparisons in total. Formatting-only edits, like converting an HTML table to a Markdown table, rejoining line breaks, switching to curly quotes, or removing bold and italic tags, were judged as ties with the original every time. On the other hand, edits that fundamentally changed document information were caught – for example, when a single digit changed, two table cells were swapped, or when two paragraphs were swapped, the judge preferred the original r-1 parse 92% - 100% of the time. ## Run your own parse evals Ultimately, the best parser for your team is one that works on your documents. With PAIR, you can evaluate parsers without writing document-specific rules or spending valuable time on human annotations. There’s no longer any reason to rely on someone else’s benchmark to choose your parser. We’re open-sourcing the evaluation frameworkhere . We also have published[ParseJudge](https://parsejudge.com/) , where you can run your own evals, compare providers, and explore parsing results. Bring your own documents and see what parser best preserves the information your workflows depend on. The PAIR judge prompt + ```text You are evaluating multiple text extractions of one PDF page. The original page image is provided for reference. The parses are blinded and shuffled. Evaluate each parse independently against the page image. ## Instructions Evaluate each extracted text against the page image. Rank each parse from best (perfect extraction) to worst (completely wrong or empty), with 0 as the best. Allow ties: equally good parses receive the same rank, including all parses receiving 0 when equally good. Use consecutive ranks for distinct quality levels (0, 1, 2, ...). Here is what you should take into account: ### Text fidelity: - Stay faithful to the visible page text, even when it appears misspelled, abbreviated, handwritten, awkward, or like a typo. Do NOT autocorrect, normalize, or silently rewrite page text while judging. - A parse should not be penalized for preserving a visible typo or unusual spelling exactly as shown on the page. Penalize only when the extracted text differs from what is visibly present. ### Tables: - Do the values in parsed document's cells match the right row, column label pairs visually in the document? - Are the rows and columns accurately captured? ### Key-value pairs: - Are the labels and values correctly paired? - For checkbox fields, are checkboxes correctly parsed as checked or unchecked? - Can you determine the values of each field from the parsed result? ### Semantic markers and placeholders: - Do not penalize a parse for using explicit markers that preserve the document's semantics even if the exact marker text is not visibly printed on the page. These include provider-specific tags for blank/empty values, unchecked or checked controls, missing optional values, signature/stamp presence, illegible text, redactions, not-applicable values, or similar normalized states. - Treat these markers as neutral formatting choices when they make the visible document state easier to recover and do not change the field, table cell, or control's meaning. - Penalize semantic markers only when they replace visible text, attach to the wrong label or cell, create a false value/state, hide that a required value is present, or make the form/table/control structure materially harder to recover. ### Reading order and block ordering: - For multi-column pages, text should be cleanly separated into columns, not merged into single lines. This is a catastrophic error. - The text should read in correct reading order, like how it would be visually inferred by a human. - Extra, repeated, or visually cluttered Markdown bullet/list markers are formatting noise when they do not change the content, reading order, or parent-child list relationships. Do NOT penalize a parse just because it has duplicated bullets such as "- -", "- o", or bullets before headings if the meaning and hierarchy remain clear. - Penalize list-marker artifacts only when they create false checkbox states, obscure text, reorder content, flatten meaningful nesting, or make parent/sub-bullet relationships materially harder to recover. ### Figures and images: - If the extraction includes a text description or summary of a figure, chart, or image on the page, do NOT penalize this. These are intentional figure summaries, not hallucinations or extraction errors. - Only penalize if the description is factually wrong about what the image shows. ### Hyperlinks and embedded URLs: - PDFs often carry hyperlink targets (e.g., mailto: addresses, https:// URLs, redirect/safelink wrappers) in a metadata layer that is not always visually rendered as text on the page. - An extraction that surfaces these embedded URLs is NOT a hallucination -- the URL genuinely exists in the PDF's link layer. - Treat hyperlink presence vs absence as a neutral formatting choice. Do NOT penalize OR reward an extraction based on whether it includes embedded URLs, markdown link syntax, or raw redirect strings. - The visible anchor TEXT itself must still match the page; only the inclusion of the underlying link target is neutral. Ignore differences in whitespace and formatting. Treat curly and straight apostrophes as equivalent. Return JSON with exactly one evaluation per label listed here: {labels} For each evaluation, include the label, a list of specific errors found, concise reasoning, and the zero-based rank. ## Parses to rank {parse_sections} ```
